studies.Population: Incident, microscopically confirmed transitional cell carcinoma of the bladder cases and hospital controls in Montevideo
studies.Smoking Status: All participants; estimates adjusted for smoking status, cigarettes per day, years since quitting, and age at smoking initiation
studies.Ethnicity Basis: NA: no field-specific ethnicity evidence was available
studies.Reference: Non-alcoholic beverages and risk of bladder cancer in Uruguay.
studies.Authors: De Stefani E, Boffetta P, Deneo-Pellegrini H, Correa P, Ronco AL, Brennan P, Ferro G, Acosta G, Mendilaharsu M
studies.Timing: Exposure assessed for usual intake five years before interview; cases were interviewed within one month of diagnosis, and recruitment occurred during 1996–2000.
studies.comparison_type: Ever tea drinkers versus never tea drinkers

sample_size.excerpt: In the time period 1996–2000, 255 incident cases with transitional cell carcinoma of the bladder and 501 patients treated in the same hospitals and in the same time period were frequency matched on age, sex, and residence.
sample_size.location: Abstract, Methods; total_n derived from reported group counts 255 + 501 = 756

cases.excerpt: In the time period 1996–2000, 255 incident cases with transitional cell carcinoma of the bladder and 501 patients treated in the same hospitals and in the same time period were frequency matched on age, sex, and residence.

effect_size.excerpt: Both coffee and tea were strongly associated with bladder cancer risk (OR for coffee drinking 1.6, 95% CI 1.2–2.3; OR for tea drinking 2.3, 95% CI 1.5–3.4).

confidence_interval.excerpt: Both coffee and tea were strongly associated with bladder cancer risk (OR for coffee drinking 1.6, 95% CI 1.2–2.3; OR for tea drinking 2.3, 95% CI 1.5–3.4).

design.excerpt: Statistical analysis was carried out by unconditional multiple logistic regression.
